title: Wuchikittawbut, Montaukett Sunksquaw
summary: Wuchikittawbut was a Montaukett sunksquaw and Wyandanch’s widow. Family deeds, the 1660 Montauk agreement, and her demand for whale payments in January 1663 reveal a leader protecting her family’s interests and negotiating with East Hampton.
content:
A Montaukett leader in her own right

Wuchikittawbut, also written Wichitaubit, was a seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw, the wife of Wyandanch and mother of Wyancombone and Quashawam. She appears in family land agreements in 1659 and continued negotiating after her husband’s death. In January 1663 she was still asserting her right to payment for whales on the South Shore.1 2

English clerks often identified her through her relationship to the “old sachem” instead of writing her name. Yet the documents give her a speaking and signing role: confirming a family agreement, answering questions about her son, and instructing boundary markers.1 2

1659–1660: the family’s agreement with Lion Gardiner

On July 14, 1659, Wuchikittawbut, Wyandanch, and Wyancombone marked the deed to Lion Gardiner concerning land between Huntington and Setauket. It connected the grant with Gardiner’s counsel and assistance in ransoming their daughter and other captives. The three family members appear together as participants in a transaction later central to Smithtown’s title history.1

After Wyandanch died, an April 6, 1660 continuation recorded the widow’s and son’s confirmation. Their participation mattered to those seeking to uphold the deed: the family’s authority and obligations continued beyond the life of its most famous sachem.1

August 1660: land, payment, and the right to return

An August 1660 Montauk indenture names Wuchikittawbut and Wyancombone alongside Pauquatoun, Cockenoe, and other Native proprietors. East Hampton’s representatives included Thomas James, Lion Gardiner, Thomas Baker, and John Mulford. The written bargain claimed the Montauk neck for the purchasers and promised £100, paid as £10 annually for ten years in corn or wampum.2

A separate counterbond addressed the Montauketts’ return to their homeland. If arrangements could be made for their safety and they wished to live there again, East Hampton promised to allow it. While they resided there, the town would withhold its payments; the English claim to the land would remain. This was a consequential condition on residence, rather than an unrestricted guarantee of continued ownership.2

1662–1663: a mother’s testimony and a demand for whale payments

On December 1, 1662, Gardiner, James, and Richard Shaw recorded her answer about Wyancombone’s age: twenty-two when he died, and twenty-one when a deed of gift was made the preceding year. The question linked his age to the validity of a land transaction. It also records that she outlived her son.2

Her declaration dated January 14, 1662/63 is especially direct. She and her son had sent Cockenoe and Tobis to mark John Cooper’s beach bounds, with Lion and David Gardiner involved. She had the limits established again that winter and expected Cooper to pay for whales coming ashore according to their covenant. She also insisted that there be no unassigned gap between Cooper’s and Anthony Waters’s bounds.2

A family’s continuing leadership

Wuchikittawbut’s final known appearances concern practical authority over land and coastal resources. Her exact birth and death dates are not recorded in these documents; the January 1663 declaration shows why she cannot simply be said to have died with her son in 1662.2 3

The following year, Quashawam appears by name in the Montaukett–Shinnecock agreement of February 11, 1663/64. Read together, mother and daughter’s records reveal successive women negotiating family interests during a period of loss and expanding colonial claims.2 3

References

  2. East Hampton records: Wyandanch agreements and canoe case. Records of the Town of East-Hampton, vol. I (1887), pp. 2–3 (1648 purchase), 172–175 (August 1660 indenture and counterbond), 198 (December 1, 1662 statement), 199–200 (January 14, 1662/63 beach agreement).
  3. Southampton II: Quashawam’s 1664 agreement and women’s 1703 land interests. The Second Book of Records of the Town of Southampton (1877), pp. 36–38 (February 11, 1663/64 agreement and John Scott authorization), 179–180 (Wiangonhut and Sumono, August 16, 1703).
why_this_matters: Wuchikittawbut centers Montaukett women's leadership. Her documented leadership shows that Native political authority was not only male and that shoreline, whaling, inheritance, and land rights were central to community survival.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
